name: Swallow Falls
blurb: Muddy Creek Falls is the tallest free-falling waterfall in Maryland at 53 feet. The mile-long loop past it runs through old-growth hemlock and white pine, some of it over 300 years old and the last of its kind in the state. It's the most visited park in Garrett County, and the reason the reservation system exists.

reservation.window: Memorial Day weekend 2026 (23 May) – Labor Day 2026
reservation.days: Weekends and holidays only. Weekdays are entry on arrival.
reservation.bookAhead: Opens 7 days before the visit; changes or cancellations until 8am the day before
reservation.note: Slots are expected to sell out consistently through the summer, so a weekend visit needs planning. On weekdays you can still turn up and pay on arrival.

fee.note: Sat of Memorial Day weekend – Labor Day: $3 per person Maryland residents, $5 per person out-of-state; Tue after Labor Day – Fri before Memorial Day: $3 per vehicle Maryland residents, $5 per vehicle out-of-state. Day-use fees are paid when you book a weekend reservation, plus a non-refundable service charge of about $1.50 per person.

Tue after Labor Day – Fri before Memorial Day

fee.passes: Maryland State Park and Trail Passport — $75 a year, $100 for non-residents. Covers day-use entry statewide. Where it can be bought in the county is not confirmed.

warnings: Pets are not permitted in the day-use area, including the Canyon Trail, from 23 May to 7 September 2026.
Alcohol is prohibited everywhere in the park except with a permit for a reserved pavilion, or inside a motor home.
Two camping units and up to six people per site, and someone in the party has to be 18 or over.

Confirm whether the main parking area restrooms are the same ones Maryland lists under the campground, or a separate day-use block — and whether they open outside camping season.
PRIORITY: confirm the day-use fee amount — every source says a fee is charged at booking, none gives the figure.
Confirm what the Park Store stocks and whether it opens outside camping season.
Resolve the county-vs-DNR conflict on whether weekdays ever need a reservation.

TWO SOURCES DISAGREE on the dog dates. This page says pets are barred from the day-use area 23 May to 7 September 2026. The 2026 printed guide says pets are only permitted there from 3 September through 24 May. Those are the same rule with different edges, and a day either way decides someone's trip. Ring the park and settle it before changing anything.

corrections.was: That a reservation was required every day from 23 May through Labor Day, not just weekends.
corrections.now: Reservations are required on weekends and holidays only; weekdays are entry on arrival. Garrett County's May announcement said every day, but Maryland DNR runs the park and the reservation system, and three DNR sources — the park page, the 20 May statewide notice and the 25 June expansion release — all say weekends and holidays. I'd followed the county.

services.officeAddress: c/o Herrington Manor State Park, 222 Herrington Lane, Oakland, MD 21550
services.note: Reported first-hand as all being at the main parking area, with the trailheads a few steps away. Maryland's campground listing separately shows restrooms, showers, a Park Store and a dump station. Whether those are the same facilities or a second set at the campground is not yet confirmed.

reports.what: The ranger station, restrooms and store are all at the main parking area, not off at the campground. The trailheads start a few steps from that same lot.

fieldNotes.author: Matt
fieldNotes.body: The ranger station, the restrooms and the store are all at the main parking area, not off at the campground the way Maryland's own listing implies. Trailheads start a few steps from the same lot, so you can park and be walking in under a minute.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer, from the 2026 printed guide
fieldNotes.body: Muddy Creek Falls is 53 feet, the highest free-falling waterfall in Maryland. Some of the hemlock and white pine along the trail is over 330 years old.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer
fieldNotes.body: Walked the trail out to Tolliver Falls. The junction sign gives Canyon Loop both ways, Muddy Creek left and Tolliver right. Tolliver is low and wide and much quieter than Muddy Creek — most people stop at the big one and turn back.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer
fieldNotes.body: The path in is crushed rock and flat enough for a rugged stroller. Worth knowing before you decide whether to carry a toddler — but only the first stretch. Past the junction it turns into steps and roots.

verdict.text: The waterfall is genuinely worth the drive, and the hemlock stand behind it is the better half. Everything you need is at the main lot, so you can park and be walking in a minute. Just don't turn up on a Saturday without a booking, because that changed in May and most of the internet hasn't noticed.

photos.alt: A wide, level crushed-stone path running straight through tall hemlock woods, with needle-covered ground on both sides.
photos.caption: The main path in from the parking area — crushed stone, level, and wide. This is the stretch a sturdy stroller will manage.

photos.alt: A wide waterfall dropping over a layered rock ledge into a brown pool, framed by summer trees on both sides and a bare rock shelf at the top left.
photos.caption: Muddy Creek Falls from the overlook, in summer. The water is tea-colored — that's tannin off the hemlocks, not silt.

photos.alt: A smaller falls seen from downstream across a broad shelf of flat wet rock, with rhododendron leaning in from both banks and a green canopy above.
photos.caption: Looking back upstream from the flat rock shelf below. Rhododendron on both banks, and the rock is slick where it looks dry.

photos.alt: A wide, low waterfall stepping over dark stacked ledges into a shallow pool, with moss and rhododendron on the bank above.
photos.caption: Tolliver Falls. Low and wide rather than tall — the opposite of Muddy Creek, and usually much quieter.

photos.alt: The same falls from downstream across a broad tea-colored pool, framed by tall hemlock and rhododendron with layered rock shelves on the right bank.
photos.caption: Tolliver from the far side of the pool. The water is that color from hemlock tannin.

photos.alt: A wooden trail sign with three arms reading Canyon Loop with arrows both ways, Muddy Creek Falls to the left and Tolliver Falls to the right, in open hemlock woods.
photos.caption: The junction that decides your walk. Muddy Creek left, Tolliver right — and note the park spells it Tolliver.

photos.alt: A narrow dirt trail with rock steps running beside a layered rock ledge hung with rhododendron, under a canopy of hemlock and birch.
photos.caption: The path along the ledge on the way to Tolliver. Rock steps, roots, and rhododendron the whole way.

photos.alt: A close view of a mossy layered rock overhang with rhododendron growing out of the cracks and a leaf-covered path at its base.
photos.caption: The ledges the trail runs under. Wet most of the year, and slick where it looks dry.

photos.alt: A small stream running through a jumble of moss-covered boulders below a steep wooded bank of hemlock and rhododendron.
photos.caption: One of the side runs coming down into the gorge.

photos.alt: A tall layered rock face with rhododendron on its ledges, and a scree of fallen slabs at its foot beside a sandy path.
photos.caption: The rock wall above the path near Tolliver. Those slabs came off the face.

photos.alt: A wide rocky river running between hemlock banks under a cloudy sky, with flat stone shelves and boulders across the near bank.
photos.caption: The Youghiogheny at the bottom of the park. This is the river the Canyon Loop follows.

onSite.label: Underfoot
onSite.note: The main path from the parking area is crushed stone, level and wide — doable with a rugged stroller. It does not stay that way: the trail out to Tolliver is rock steps, roots and ledges.

onSite.label: The campground
onSite.note: 65 sites with modern bath houses, fire rings, lantern posts and stabilized pads. Three sites have sewer, water and electric; three more have water and electric.

onSite.label: Camper cabins
onSite.note: Three, each with a double bed and a bunk bed, a mini-fridge and a microwave.

onSite.label: Picnicking
onSite.note: Tables and grills past the main parking area, on the hill. The pavilion beside the main lot can be rented.

onSite.label: The walk
onSite.note: A mile and a quarter loop past Muddy Creek, Swallow, and Upper and Lower Tolliver Falls. A separate 5.5-mile trail connects the park to Herrington Manor.

onSite.label: Booking
onSite.note: 888-432-2267 Monday to Friday, or parkreservations.maryland.gov. The park itself is reachable year round on 301-334-9180.

name: Deep Creek Lake
blurb: The state park sits on the northeast shore of Maryland's largest lake, with the only public swimming beach on Deep Creek and a discovery center that stays open year-round. Everything else on the lake is private shoreline, which is why this one gets busy.

reservation.note: Not on Maryland DNR's list of parks requiring day-use reservations as of 25 June 2026. Day-use fees may still apply on arrival.

fee.note: Memorial Day weekend – Labor Day: $3 per person Maryland residents, $5 per person out-of-state; Day after Labor Day – Fri before Memorial Day: $3 per vehicle Maryland residents, $5 per vehicle out-of-state.

schedule.when: Day after Labor Day – Fri before Memorial Day

fee.passes: Maryland State Park and Trail Passport — $75 a year, $100 for non-residents. Covers day-use entry statewide. Where it can be bought in the county is not confirmed.

warnings: Dogs are allowed, but not on the beach. The one part of this park most people drive here for is the part the dog can't come to.
Jet skis and other personal watercraft cannot run 11am to 4pm on Saturdays, Sundays and holidays from 1 July to Labor Day.
There is a service charge to launch a boat. It covers launching and removal in one 24-hour period.
This is a trash-free park. There are no bins and no recycling. Whatever you bring in, you carry out.

photos.alt: A child in a sun hat crouched at the water's edge with a bucket, on a sand beach inside a long stone breakwater, with wooded hills across the lake and the sun flaring through a big tree.
photos.caption: Late afternoon at the beach, inside the breakwater. The shade at the back of the sand is already gone by this point in the day.

photos.alt: A wide sand beach curving to a lake, with stone breakwaters enclosing a swim area, people swimming and sitting on the sand, and forested hills along the far shore.
photos.caption: The swim area, enclosed by stone breakwaters. DNR lists two sandy beaches here; this is the one people mean.

reports.what: Photographed the beach area — sand, an enclosed swim area behind stone breakwaters, and open lake beyond.
There are showers at the park.
Dogs are allowed at the park, but not on the beach.

fieldNotes.author: Matt
fieldNotes.body: The swim area is roped inside stone breakwaters, so it stays calm even when the rest of the lake is busy with boats. Plenty of sand, and shade at the back of the beach if you get there early enough to claim it.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer, from the 2026 printed guide
fieldNotes.body: Facts about the lake, from the park's own guide: 65 miles of shoreline, 3,900 acres, average depth 26.5 feet, surface 73F in summer and 49F on the bottom. Meadow Mountain tops out at 3,022 feet.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer
fieldNotes.body: The visitor FAQ board at the Discovery Center confirms the entry fees this page already listed, and adds the thing nobody publishes: no bins anywhere in the park. It also names the duty ranger's number, which is the one to use when the office is shut.

verdict.text: The swim area sits inside stone breakwaters, so it stays flat even when the rest of the lake is full of boats. Plenty of sand. The shade at the back of the beach goes early, though.

onSite.label: Ranger station
onSite.note: At the junction of Brant and State Park Roads. Hunting and fishing licenses are sold here.

onSite.label: The campground
onSite.note: Meadow Mountain: 112 sites, open 15 April to 15 December. Heated restrooms with hot water showers. Twenty-six sites have 30-amp electric and water. Dump station at the entrance.

onSite.label: Sleeping without a tent
onSite.note: A yurt, two mini camper-cabins, and the Bear Den, which is an Adirondack-style shelter.

onSite.label: Booking
onSite.note: parkreservations.maryland.gov or 888-432-2267. Two weeks is the longest stay.

onSite.label: The beach
onSite.note: The only guarded public swimming beach on the lake, guarded Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day weekend.

onSite.label: Boat launch
onSite.note: Outside the day-use area on State Park Road. The canoe and kayak launch is inside the day-use area. Open 24 hours except when ice or weather closes it.

onSite.label: Trails
onSite.note: The Meadow Mountain system is over 20 miles, from level to steep. Maps at park headquarters or the Discovery Center.

onSite.label: Getting to headquarters
onSite.note: Turn right out of the Discovery Center parking lot and take the next left. If you cross the bridge you've gone too far.

onSite.label: Beach parking
onSite.note: Turn left out of the Discovery Center parking lot, next left, and stop at the contact station.

onSite.label: Best trail
onSite.note: The park's own FAQ board names Beckmans as the most recommended trail here. Check the map for length and difficulty.

onSite.label: Boat tours
onSite.note: Run by Wisp but launched from the Discovery Center dock. Book ahead on 844-369-2485.

onSite.label: Numbers
onSite.note: Camp office 301-387-5563. Discovery Center 301-387-7067. Duty ranger 240-405-9827.

name: Herrington Manor
blurb: A 53-acre lake made by damming Herrington Creek, with twenty year-round cabins built by the Civilian Conservation Corps. No gas motors on the lake, which keeps it quiet. Cross-country ski rental in winter, one of very few places in Maryland where that's a real option.

reservation.note: Not on Maryland DNR's list of parks requiring day-use reservations as of 25 June 2026. Day-use fees may still apply on arrival.

fee.note: Summer weekends, and ski-season weekends and holidays: $3 per person Maryland residents, $5 per person out-of-state; Weekdays: $3 per vehicle Maryland residents, $5 per vehicle out-of-state.

warnings: Dogs are allowed on the trails and in the day-use area, but NOT on the sandy part of the beach, in the swimming area, or inside buildings.

name: New Germany
blurb: A 13-acre lake on the site of a nineteenth-century milling settlement, wrapped inside Savage River State Forest. Eleven cabins, a groomed cross-country ski network in winter, and enough elevation that it holds snow when the rest of Maryland has none.

reservation.note: Not on Maryland DNR's list of parks requiring day-use reservations as of 25 June 2026. Day-use fees may still apply on arrival.

fee.note: No day-use service charge listed by Maryland DNR as of 3 August 2026.
fee.passes: Maryland State Park and Trail Passport — $75 a year, $100 for non-residents. Covers day-use entry statewide. Where it can be bought in the county is not confirmed.

warnings: New Germany is replacing its water and waste water treatment plant in 2026-2027. Cabins, campsites and pavilions will close at various times during construction and the park says closures are subject to change. Ring 301-895-5453 before booking.

onSite.label: Cabins
onSite.note: Twelve log cabins, bookable year round, each with electric heat, a wood stove, a full kitchen and a bathroom. Pets are allowed in cabins 3 to 7 only.

onSite.label: The campground
onSite.note: Forty sites. Site 34 has 30-amp electric. The Alpine Lodge (site 40) is an Adirondack-style shelter sleeping ten. Sites 3 and 31 are safari-style glamping tents on raised platforms.

onSite.label: Showers
onSite.note: The White Oak Loop shower house is heated and open year round. It's pet friendly.

onSite.label: The lake
onSite.note: Thirteen acres, with a designated swimming area and a free swim beach. Kayaks, canoes and paddle boards to rent at the Lake House or Ranger Station. Gasoline motors are prohibited.

onSite.label: Trails
onSite.note: More than ten miles, easy to moderate, well signed and intersecting often so you can shorten a route.

onSite.label: Shelters
onSite.note: Two picnic pavilions. Tall Oaks takes 75 and has a wood-burning fireplace; Tamarack takes 40 and sits by the playground.

onSite.label: Indoors
onSite.note: The Black Forest Room in the Lake House holds 60 and can be reserved. The gift shop in the Ranger Station sells firewood, licenses and clothing, 8am to 4pm daily, year round.

onSite.label: Winter
onSite.note: Trails are tracked and groomed for skiing. Skis and snowshoes to rent. Ice fishing is allowed on the lake. They call the sledding hills the Maryland Alps.

name: Big Run
blurb: Three hundred acres at the mouth of the Savage River where it meets the reservoir, surrounded on all sides by Savage River State Forest. Primitive camping, and the put-in for some of the most serious whitewater in the mid-Atlantic when the river is released.

reservation.note: Not on Maryland DNR's list of parks requiring day-use reservations as of 25 June 2026. Day-use fees may still apply on arrival.

fee.note: No day-use service charge listed by Maryland DNR as of 3 August 2026.
fee.passes: Maryland State Park and Trail Passport — $75 a year, $100 for non-residents. Covers day-use entry statewide. Where it can be bought in the county is not confirmed.

warnings: Whitewater here depends on scheduled dam releases from the Savage River Reservoir. Without a release there may be no runnable water at all.
No potable water and no trash service. Bring water in and carry rubbish out.
Big Run does NOT have cell service.
Swimming and gas-powered boats are prohibited in the Savage River Reservoir.
Pets must be leashed and with their owner.

onSite.label: Trails

onSite.note: The Friends Store and the Election House were the center of the Sang Run community until the 1970s. The Friend family farmed here from the early 1800s until the state bought it in 2008.

onSite.label: Walking
onSite.note: The Bluebird Trail, and demonstration gardens around the park.

onSite.label: Picnic shelter
onSite.note: Rentable for larger gatherings.

fieldNotes.author: Site maintainer, from the 2026 printed guide
fieldNotes.body: The Election House ties to the campaign for the 19th Amendment — the guide says Garrett County helped propel the suffrage movement, and the house is where that is told.

name: Wolf Den Run
blurb: Maryland's designated off-highway vehicle park, on reclaimed mine land above the Potomac's north branch. Miles of ATV and dirt bike trail, plus hiking, fishing and hunting. Unlike anywhere else in the state park system.

reservation.note: OHV parks usually require a separate permit rather than a day-use reservation. Unconfirmed.

name: Youghiogheny Wild River
blurb: Maryland's only designated wild river, running north through a gorge toward Pennsylvania. Managed for the river rather than for visitors, so there are few facilities. The whitewater through here is among the hardest in the east.

name: Savage River State Forest
blurb: Maryland's largest state forest at around 54,000 acres, wrapping Big Run and New Germany. Dispersed camping, hunting, trout water and the reservoir behind it. A forest rather than a park, which means different rules. Worth knowing which one you're standing in.

name: Rock Maze
blurb: A natural labyrinth of house-sized sandstone boulders, moss over every surface, with passages narrow enough to turn sideways for. It isn't a signed DNR trail and it isn't on the state forest's map. Locals know it, and that's mostly how you find it.

reservation.note: Not on Maryland DNR's list of parks requiring day-use reservations as of 25 June 2026.

warnings: Snaggy Mountain Road is one of the forest's ORV trail areas. Expect motorised vehicles on the road you park on.
There is no sign, no marked trailhead and no facilities. The parking area is small.
The boulders are moss-covered and hold water. They are slick well after rain, and the passages between them are genuinely tight.

reports.what: The trailhead is a small parking area on Snaggy Mountain Road, near where it meets Cranesville Road. The walk in runs through open hardwood with heavy fern cover before it reaches the boulders.

photos.alt: Two children walking away from the camera down a narrow passage between two towering moss-covered sandstone walls, with daylight above.
photos.caption: The passage itself. The walls are what the name is about, and the figures are there for scale — several of the gaps are barely shoulder-width.

photos.alt: A narrow earth footpath running through open hardwood forest, banked on both sides by dense waist-high ferns, with sunlight coming through the canopy.
photos.caption: The approach: open hardwood and heavy fern cover before the ground turns to boulders.

photos.alt: A tree growing directly out of a large moss-covered sandstone boulder, its roots running down the rock face, with rhododendron around it.
photos.caption: Sandstone under moss, with trees rooted straight over the rock. This is the surface the whole maze is made of — and why it stays slick.

photos.alt: Several pink-capped Russula mushrooms growing on dark leaf litter on the forest floor.
photos.caption: Russula on the forest floor in early August. Look, photograph, do not eat.

fieldNotes.author: Matt
fieldNotes.body: The trailhead is a small pull-in on Snaggy Mountain Road near Cranesville Road. No sign, so you are looking for the parking area rather than the trail. The walk in is open hardwood with fern up to your knees, and then the ground turns to boulders fairly suddenly. Some of the passages are barely shoulder-width and everything is mossy, which means slick long after it has stopped raining. Not one to do in a hurry.

verdict.text: House-sized boulders with passages between them narrow enough to turn sideways for, and no sign anywhere telling you it exists. The moss holds water for days, so it's slick long after the rain stops. Not one to rush, and not one to do in trainers.

name: Jennings Randolph Lake
blurb: A five-mile reservoir on the North Branch of the Potomac, holding back water for Washington DC since 1981 and forming the Maryland-West Virginia line. Over a hundred feet deep, and it holds the state walleye record. Run jointly by Swallow Falls and Herrington Manor with the Army Corps of Engineers.

fee.note: Not confirmed. The guide names no fee for the boat ramp.

warnings: The boat ramp is open April through October, weather permitting. It is not a year-round launch.
The lake is the state line. Which side you fish from decides whose license you need — unconfirmed which applies where.

onSite.label: Boat ramp
onSite.note: Open April through October, weather permitting. A floating dock, and parking for 50 boat trailers.

onSite.label: Fishing
onSite.note: State record walleye, caught here in 1998. Over 100 feet deep, so bring enough rope for your anchor line.
